hmmt-feb-2024-comb-01.title: Vertical lines force columns
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-01.body:
Let the side of length $20$ be vertical. Any vertical line through the rectangle crosses tiles whose heights (each $4$ or $5$) add to $20$: either $4+4+4+4+4$ or $5+5+5+5$. These correspond to full-height columns of tiles: five tiles of height $4$ (a column of width $5$) or four tiles of height $5$ (a column of width $4$). So the tiling is a row of such columns, and we just need the column widths to add up to $24$.

So we need to write $24$ as an ordered sum of $4$'s and $5$'s: $4+4+4+4+4+4$ ($1$ way) or one $4$ and four $5$'s ($5$ orders). Total $1+5=6$.

**Answer: 6**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-01.title: Exhaustive search
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-01.body:
A backtracking search (fill the top-left empty cell with a $4\times5$ or $5\times4$ tile) finds exactly $6$ tilings of the $20\times24$ rectangle.

**Answer: 6**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-02.title: Column coloring
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-02.body:
Every move goes to an adjacent column. Color the columns alternately black and white, starting with black; the king alternates colors, starting on black. There are $4\cdot7=28$ black and $3\cdot7=21$ white cells, so a path visits at most $21$ white cells and $22$ black cells: at most $43$ cells.

**Construction.** Columns 1–2 downward: $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(2,2),\dots,(7,1),(7,2)$ (row, column) — each step is horizontal or diagonal. Then columns 3–4 upward: $(7,3),(7,4),(6,3),(6,4),\dots,(1,3),(1,4)$; then columns 5–6 downward: $(1,5),(1,6),\dots,(7,5),(7,6)$; finally $(7,7)$. That is $14\cdot3+1=43$ cells.

**Answer: 43**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-02.title: Why 44 is impossible
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-02.body:
In any path the colors alternate, so the numbers of black and white cells differ by at most one. With only $21$ white cells, at most $22$ black cells can be used, so at most $43$ in total, and the zigzag path above achieves this.

**Answer: 43**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-03.title: Casework on positions
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-03.body:
A corner cube shows on $3$ faces, an edge cube on $2$, a face-center on $1$, the center on $0$. We need the two red cubes to show on $4$ faces in total (as a union).
- Two corners: they cover $4$ faces only if they are adjacent (share an edge of the big cube): $12$ ways.
- Corner $+$ edge: $8$ corners; the edge cube must add exactly one new face, i.e. lie on one of the three faces at the corner the edge cube must lie on exactly one of the three faces at the corner: $6$ edges. $8\cdot6=48$.
- Corner $+$ face center: the face must be one of the $3$ faces not touching the corner: $8\cdot3=24$.
- Two edges: they must cover $4$ different faces: $12$ choices, then $5$ edges sharing no face with it, divided by $2$: $30$.
- Other combinations show on at most $3$ faces.

Total $12+48+24+30=114$.

**Answer: 114**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-03.title: Brute force
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-03.body:
There are $\binom{27}2=351$ ways to choose the two red positions. For each, compute the set of big-cube faces on which some red cube lies; exactly $114$ of them give $4$ faces.

**Answer: 114**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-04.title: Two branches and a doubling
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-04.body:
Picture $j$ as the column index. From $(2,1)$ Sally must step to $(1,1)$ or $(3,1)$ (continuing to $(2,2)$ would strand one of the corners); by symmetry say $(3,1)$, and multiply by $2$ at the end. Then the corner $(1,1)$ can only be the end of the path.

Follow the path from the start and backwards from the end: both branches move along the outer rows into column $2$. In each pair of columns, exactly one of the branches dips into the middle row and fills it back, and the configuration for the remaining columns is the same as before with two fewer columns. Each such step offers $2$ choices. With $24=2\cdot12$ columns this gives $2\cdot2^{11}=2^{12}=4096$ paths.

**Answer: 4096**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-04.title: Small cases and a stars-and-bars count
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-04.body:
For a $3\times2n$ lattice the count is $2^n$. Counting by the number $k$ of returns to the middle row (blocks), one gets $2\sum_{k=1}^{n}\binom{n-1}{k-1}=2\cdot2^{n-1}=2^n$. A computer enumeration of Hamiltonian paths from the middle of the first column gives $2,4,8,16,32$ for $n=1,\dots,5$, confirming the pattern. For $n=12$: $2^{12}=4096$.

**Answer: 4096**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-05.title: Two copies of $K_4$ or a cube
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-05.body:
The graph is $3$-regular and any two vertices have $0$ or $2$ common neighbours. Let vertex $1$ have neighbours $2,3,4$.

- If two of $2,3,4$ are adjacent, say $2\sim3$: then $1$ and $3$ share neighbour $2$, so they share a second one, which must be $4$. Similarly $2\sim4$. So $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is a $K_4$, and the other four cities form another $K_4$. There are $\frac12\binom84=35$ such graphs.
- Otherwise $2,3,4$ are pairwise non-adjacent. Each pair among them shares $1$, so shares exactly one more neighbour; these three extra neighbours are distinct (one vertex adjacent to all of $2,3,4$ would share $3$ neighbours with $1$). The last vertex is adjacent to those three. This is the cube graph $Q_3$. It has $48$ automorphisms, so there are $\frac{8!}{48}=840$ labelings.

Total $35+840=875$.

**Answer: 875**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-05.title: Computer enumeration
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-05.body:
Enumerating all labeled $3$-regular graphs on $8$ vertices and testing the common-neighbour condition for every pair gives exactly $875$ graphs.

**Answer: 875**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-06.title: Even degree at interior vertices
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-06.body:
**Claim.** A valid coloring exists iff every interior grid vertex meets an even number of drawn segments (grid lines plus diagonals).

If some interior vertex has odd degree, the regions around it form an odd cycle of alternating colors — impossible. Conversely, if all interior vertices are even, the coloring can be built (a standard parity argument).

Each interior vertex has the $4$ grid edges plus $0$–$4$ diagonals ending there, so the number of diagonals at it must be even. Given the diagonals in the top row and left column ($7$ cells), the diagonals in the remaining $9$ cells are determined one by one: for cells $(2,2),(2,3),\dots$, three of the four cells around the vertex at their top-left corner are known, and parity fixes the fourth. So each of the remaining $9$ cells has exactly one allowed choice, and the probability is $\frac1{2^9}=\frac1{512}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{512}$**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-06.title: Exhaustive check
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-06.body:
For each of the $2^{16}$ choices of diagonals, build the adjacency graph of the $32$ triangles and test whether it is bipartite. Exactly $128=2^7$ choices work, giving probability $\frac{128}{65536}=\frac1{512}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{512}$**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-07.title: Recursion on the first column
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-07.body:
Label cells $(x,y)$, $y\in\{0,1\}$, $x\ge0$, with Philip at $(0,0)$. Let $W$ be the door $(0,0)$–$(0,1)$, $X$ the door $(0,0)$–$(1,0)$, $Y$ the door $(0,1)$–$(1,1)$. Let $A$ ($B$) be the expected count given $W$ unlocked (locked); the answer is $\frac{A+B}2$.

**$W$ unlocked.** Both cells of column $0$ are reachable.
- $X,Y$ both locked (prob. $\frac14$): $2$ cells.
- Both unlocked ($\frac14$): like the case $A$ shifted by one column, plus $2$: $A+2$.
- Exactly one unlocked ($\frac12$): like the original problem from one corner of column $1$, plus $2$: $\frac{A+B}2+2$.

So $A=\frac14\cdot2+\frac14(A+2)+\frac12\left(\frac{A+B}2+2\right)$.

**$W$ locked.**
- $X$ locked ($\frac12$): $1$ cell.
- $X$ unlocked, $Y$ locked ($\frac14$): $\frac{A+B}2+1$.
- $X,Y$ unlocked ($\frac14$): $\frac{A+B}2+1$ plus the cell $(0,1)$ if $(1,1)$ is reachable from $(1,0)$. That happens with probability $\sum_{n\ge0}\frac1{2^{3n+1}}=\frac47$ (go right $n$ columns along the bottom, then up, then back along the top: $3n+1$ doors).

So $B=\frac12+\frac14\left(\frac{A+B}2+1\right)+\frac14\left(\frac{A+B}2+1+\frac47\right)$.

Solving: $A=\frac{40}7$, $B=\frac{24}7$, and the answer is $\frac{A+B}2=\frac{32}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{32}{7}$**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-07.title: Truncated grids converge
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-07.body:
Computing the expectation exactly for grids of length $L=2,3,\dots,7$ (all $2^{3L-2}$ door configurations) gives $2.5625,\ 3.258,\ 3.712,\ 4.009,\ 4.203,\ 4.330$. The increments shrink geometrically (ratio about $0.65$), and extrapolating gives a limit of about $4.57\approx\frac{32}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{32}{7}$**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-08.title: Recursion on the number of pairs
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-08.body:
Let $E_n$ be the expected number of socks drawn (including the final pair) with $n$ pairs; $E_1=2$. Imagine drawing the whole drawer and let the last sock be red. Ignoring both red socks, the process is the $(n-1)$-pair process; let it stop after $k$ socks. The first red sock is equally likely to be in any of the $2n-1$ gaps among the other socks; it lies before that stopping point with probability $\frac{k}{2n-1}$, and then it is counted as well. So $E_n=E_{n-1}\left(1+\frac1{2n-1}\right)=\frac{2n}{2n-1}E_{n-1}$, giving
$$E_n=\frac{2\cdot4\cdots2n}{1\cdot3\cdots(2n-1)}=\frac{4^n(n!)^2}{(2n)!}=\frac{4^n}{\binom{2n}n}.$$
Subtracting the final pair, the expected number of unpaired socks is $\dfrac{4^{2024}}{\binom{4048}{2024}}-2$ (about $77.7$).

**Answer: $\dfrac{4^{2024}}{\binom{4048}{2024}}-2$**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-08.title: Tail sums
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-08.body:
Let $P(k)$ be the probability that more than $k$ socks are drawn, i.e. the first $k$ are pairwise different:
$$P(k)=\frac{4048\cdot4046\cdots(4050-2k)}{4048\cdot4047\cdots(4049-k)}=\frac{2^k\binom{4048-k}{2024}}{\binom{4048}{2024}}.$$
The expected number drawn is $\sum_{k=0}^{2024}P(k)$. The identity $\sum_{k=0}^{2024}2^k\binom{4048-k}{2024}=4^{2024}$ holds by counting subsets of $\{1,\dots,4049\}$ with at least $2025$ elements ($2^{4048}$ of them, by symmetry) according to the position $k+1$ of the $2025$th largest chosen element. So the expected number drawn is $\frac{4^{2024}}{\binom{4048}{2024}}$, and the answer is that minus $2$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{4^{2024}}{\binom{4048}{2024}}-2$**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-09.title: Reduce to involutions
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-09.body:
Write composition as multiplication. The conditions are $fgh=hgf=g$, $ghf=fhg=h$, $hfg=gfh=f$. Then
$$f=gfh=(fgh)fh=fghfh=f(ghf)h=fhh,$$
so $h^2=1$; similarly $f^2=g^2=1$. From $fgh=g$: $fg=gh^{-1}=gh$; likewise $gh=hf$. Let $x=fg=gh=hf$; then $x^3=(fg)(gh)(hf)=1$. Conversely, involutions with $fg=gh=hf$ satisfy all the conditions.

- $x=1$: $f=g=h$ is any involution of $\{1,\dots,5\}$: $1+\binom52+\frac12\binom{5}{2,2,1}=1+10+15=26$.
- $x\ne1$: $x$ is a $3$-cycle ($20$ choices), say $(1\,2\,3)$. Then $f,g,h$ preserve $\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{4,5\}$; on $\{1,2,3\}$ they are the three transpositions in one of $3$ cyclic arrangements, and on $\{4,5\}$ they are all the identity or all the swap ($2$ ways). So $20\cdot6=120$.

Total $26+120=146$.

**Answer: 146**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-09.title: Brute force
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-09.body:
Checking all $120^3\approx1.7$ million triples of permutations against the six identities by computer gives exactly $146$ solutions.

**Answer: 146**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-10.title: Carries and a bijection
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-10.body:
Count peacocks $x$ with $2x$ a peacock. Doubling digit $d$ gives $2d$ or $2d+1$ (with a carry in) mod $10$; digits $d$ and $d+5$ give the same even digit. So $2x$ uses all ten digits iff exactly one digit of each pair $(0,5),(1,6),(2,7),(3,8),(4,9)$ receives a carry. A carry comes from the next digit to the right being $\ge5$. Also the leading digit of $x$ must be $\le4$.

Encode $x$ by: the order of the "low" digits $0$–$4$ in $x$ (with $0$ not first), the order of the "high" digits $5$–$9$, and which digit of each pair is marked as receiving a carry. Rebuild $x$ by starting with the low queue and, after each digit, taking the next high digit if the current digit is marked and the next low digit otherwise. One checks this is a bijection onto valid $x$, provided the last high digit is not marked (the last digit of $x$ receives no carry).

Count: low order $4\cdot4!$ (0 not first), high order $5!$, and markings $2^4$ (the pair containing the last high digit is forced). Total $4\cdot24\cdot120\cdot16=184320$.

**Answer: 184320**

hmmt-feb-2024-comb-10.title: Brute force
hmmt-feb-2024-comb-10.body:
Loop over all $10$-digit pandigital numbers $x$ with leading digit $1$–$4$ and check whether $2x$ is again pandigital: exactly $184320$ such $x$ exist, so $184320$ peacocks are twice another peacock.

**Answer: 184320**
